analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority over tobacco and requires companies to meet targets for reducing children's tobacco use.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced with 45 cosponsors, no further action was taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given the Food and Drug Administration legal authority over tobacco products, treating nicotine as a drug and tobacco products as devices under food and drug law. It would have restricted tobacco advertising and marketing, required smoke-free policies in public facilities, forced manufacturers to hit annual targets for reducing tobacco use among children (with price increases and sales restrictions as penalties for missing them), and spent $800 million on anti-tobacco campaigns and enforcement. States that failed to adopt a model tobacco-control program could lose up to 20 percent of their federal tobacco-control funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, who would face tighter marketing restrictions, licensing of sellers, required reductions in child tobacco use, and a $500 million national campaign to discourage tobacco use [S2, S3]. Nonsmoking adults and children, who would get smoke-free policies in public facilities enforceable by citizens in court [S3]. Minority communities, whose tobacco use levels the bill required HHS to track and report on specifically [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and nonsmoking adults exposed to smoke

how_it_helps.text: Gives the FDA jurisdiction over tobacco products as drugs and devices, validating the 1996 FDA rule, and mandates additional restrictions on tobacco marketing, advertising, and youth access drawn from the 1997 proposed tobacco settlement

Requires each manufacturer to cut its rate of child tobacco use on a fixed schedule — at least 33 percent below baseline by years 3-4, rising to 80 percent by year 10 — with escalating penalties for missing targets, including required price increases whose proceeds fund anti-tobacco enforcement and education
Requires smoke-free policies in public facilities, enforceable by any aggrieved person in court with up to $5,000 per day in civil penalties

Funds a $500 million national public-awareness campaign against tobacco use and $300 million for enforcement, with campaigns required to be culturally and linguistically appropriate for minority populations

Conditions federal tobacco-control funding on states adopting a model tobacco-control program, including retailer licensing and compliance inspections, with up to 20 percent of funding withheld from noncompliant states
Requires HHS to measure child tobacco use among minority populations annually and report to Congress with recommendations if use is rising or falling too slowly in any group

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would bear mandated price increases that are paid over to the Treasury when they miss child-use targets, plus the cost of marketing restrictions, warning changes, and ingredient disclosures. Retailers and broadcasters would lose tobacco advertising and single-pack sales for penalized brands. Some of the required price increases would also be paid by adult smokers at the register. Taxpayers would fund $800 million for the public-awareness campaign and enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The penalty mechanism is mandatory price increases, which are paid partly by adult smokers at the register — including low-income smokers — before the money reaches the Treasury

Treating tobacco as a drug and device and restricting advertising raises unresolved First Amendment questions; the bill itself instructs the Secretary to exclude any marketing restriction that would violate the First Amendment, an implicit acknowledgment of the legal risk
The bill appropriates $800 million for campaigns and enforcement and creates an annual national survey of children's tobacco use, a new and recurring federal undertaking

The smoke-free mandate covers nearly any building where interstate commerce occurs, which some would view as an overbroad federal mandate on private property owners, though it exempts bars, private clubs, prisons, and tobacco shops

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefits would have been large and the structure unusually enforceable: quantified annual reduction targets for child tobacco use, citizen lawsuits to enforce smoke-free facilities, and penalties that fund their own enforcement. The main costs fall on the tobacco industry by design; the costs that reach ordinary people are higher cigarette prices passed through to adult smokers and $800 million in federal spending. The design is aggressive but not careless — it builds in First Amendment carve-outs, judicial review, and state flexibility with funding consequences.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Waxman introduced the bill on March 15, 2001 with 45 cosponsors, including two Republicans
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day
That referral was the last action of any kind; no hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, who faced no new FDA jurisdiction, no mandated child-use reductions, and no advertising restrictions; the committee and its leadership were also spared a politically difficult vote. The status quo of the time, in which the FDA's claimed authority over tobacco had been struck down in court, continued.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 45 original cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place before the Congress ended

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee action during the 107th Congress

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 43 of 208 House Democrats cosponsored versus just 2 of 223 House Republicans — and the bill died in the Republican-run Energy and Commerce Committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill is built around them: FDA jurisdiction, mandated reductions in child tobacco use, advertising bans, and escalating price penalties paid into the Treasury for every missed target. The industry's interest in avoiding these measures runs directly against the public-health purpose of the bill.

The bill would require state retailer licensing, compliance inspections, and license suspension or revocation, and would bar sale of penalized brands in quantities smaller than a carton. Some retailers profit from underage sales, which the restrictions target.

The bill bans tobacco advertising on any medium under FCC jurisdiction and requires stronger warning labels, ending a lucrative advertising category. The bill itself exempts any restriction it deems would violate the First Amendment.
